title: Arctic Inference SuffixDecodingCache source (cache.py)
quote: Also update the response if the request is in the global cache ... the new tokens can be used for future speculations for all requests
proves: The one global suffix tree is keyed only by an internal seq_id generated from req_id; add_active_response feeds every request's sampled tokens into _global_tree, and speculate() queries both the per-request local tree and the shared global tree and returns whichever draft scores higher. No tenant, LoRA, or salt field exists; any request can draft from any earlier request's output.
does_not_prove: Does not show an actual cross-tenant recovery; correctness of final output is preserved by target verification, so the channel is only through acceptance/timing.
bearing: C5 mechanism: confirms shared tenant-blind draft cache in code

title: Arctic Inference suffix_tree.cc (_speculate_path / count-based prob)
proves: Draft selection walks the most-frequent child path (head_child) and multiplies frequency ratios; a token is only drafted while running prob >= min_token_prob (default 0.1) and match grows the budget via max_spec_factor*match_len. So a victim span is proposable from the global tree only if it occurred often enough that its frequency estimate clears 0.1 for each step and the attacker supplies the matching context prefix.
does_not_prove: Does not quantify how many victim repetitions are needed to clear min_token_prob in a mixed batch; single-occurrence victim spans with common prefixes may fall below threshold.
bearing: C5 feasibility: a probe triggers a victim draft only above a frequency/prob threshold

title: vLLM RFC #51788: Suffix decoding on GPU (suffix_gpu)
quote: a per-request local matcher plus a cross-request global suffix index (the analogue of the CPU method's global tree / max_cached_requests)
proves: The cross-request global draft index is being reimplemented GPU-resident for async scheduling; measured AL rises 1.53->2.33 (c1->c256) only because the global index compounds under concurrent traffic, confirming the cross-request benefit is real and grows with batch/concurrency. Still per-process, no tenant namespace.
does_not_prove: Does not add any isolation; does not measure leakage. Benefit over per-request tree shown only on Spec-Bench, not a multi-tenant mix.
bearing: C5/C8: cross-request global tree benefit grows with concurrency; still tenant-blind

title: Arctic Inference issue #185: suffix decoding perf degradation under high concurrency
quote: this is expected for speculative decoding since high-concurrency scenarios leave less compute for verifying speculations
proves: Maintainer confirms suffix decoding net-loses throughput above ~batch 20 because verifying rejected drafts costs compute; the standard mitigation is disable_by_batch_size (turn speculation off above a batch threshold). Rejected drafts still consume verification FLOPs.
does_not_prove: Does not address leakage; shows the channel's benefit regime (low/medium batch) is exactly where the attack would also be strongest, but at high batch spec is often off entirely.
bearing: C5 scale attack: cross-request gain and channel both shrink or get disabled at high batch

title: Arctic Inference issue #261: saving SuffixDecodingCache for future use
quote: The current implementation seems to only work for a single process.
proves: Confirms the suffix cache (global tree) is per-process in-memory state, unpicklable, not shared or persisted across replicas/sessions.
does_not_prove: Does not discuss cross-replica sharing design; only notes it is absent.
bearing: C8: each replica/process holds a separate tree; no cross-replica sharing exists

title: Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs
quote: We detect global cache sharing across users in seven API providers
proves: Establishes that cross-user (global) cache sharing is real in production and timing-detectable, in seven providers including OpenAI's embedding model. Precedent that a shared cache that crosses users is a genuine, measurable side channel.
does_not_prove: Concerns prefix/KV prompt caching, not draft/suffix caches; does not test speculative decoding.
bearing: C5 relevance/novelty: cross-user cache leakage is real in prod but only shown for prefix cache

title: InputSnatch / Auditing lineage: CacheProbe: Auditing Prompt Cache Isolation in Gateway APIs
quote: inadvertently create global cache sharing across all OpenRouter users
proves: Shows isolation scope (per-account/per-org vs global) is the security-relevant variable and that gateways can collapse per-org isolation into global sharing. Frames the hit/miss latency gap as the channel.
does_not_prove: Prefix cache only; no draft/suffix cache; page is abstract-only, no results quoted.
bearing: C5: isolation-scope framing transfers to draft caches but unproven there

title: Governing/Selective KV-Cache Sharing (SafeKV) to mitigate timing side-channels
quote: most of the performance benefits of global sharing
proves: A selective/per-trust-group sharing defence keeps most of global sharing's benefit while cutting TTFT isolation overhead up to 40.58% and raising throughput up to 2.66x. Demonstrates the 'salt/partition by trust group keeps most benefit' defence pattern C5 proposes, for prefix cache.
does_not_prove: For KV/prefix cache, not draft caches; does not prove the same retention holds for a suffix draft tree where cross-tenant hits may matter more or less.
bearing: C5 baseline defence: per-trust-group partition keeps most benefit (prefix-cache evidence)

title: Characterizing Contention-Induced Reliability Collapse in KV-Cache Timing Side Channels
quote: mean Cohen's d drops from 0.7789 with no synthetic workers to 0.2109 with two workers
proves: Concurrent load collapses KV-cache timing-channel reliability: effect size 0.78->0.21 with two synthetic workers, AUROC 0.650->0.531, and on 2-node TP vLLM mean d 3.418->0.511. 'Measurements on quiet systems can overestimate operational attack reliability.'
does_not_prove: Studies KV-cache timing, not draft-cache acceptance or streamed-chunk-count channels; streaming chunk counts (accepted tokens per step) are not a pure timing channel and may survive contention.
bearing: C5 scale attack: realistic batching may blur a TIMING channel; chunk-count channel untested

title: Detokenization Leaks: Reconstructing Local LLM Outputs From Cache Traces
quote: observing CPU cache activity during detokenization
proves: A separate output-reconstruction channel exists via CPU cache of the detokenizer, independent of speculation; recovers semantically accurate outputs across frameworks and model families.
does_not_prove: Requires co-located process sharing tokenizer code pages, not a remote co-tenant through a shared draft cache; does not involve suffix/n-gram caches.
bearing: C5 adjacent: output leakage via a different channel; does not scoop the draft-cache question

title: WAR: Workload-Aware Rollouts for Synchronous Agentic Reinforcement Learning
quote: In RL training, each rollout worker maintains its own suffix tree independently.
proves: Directly addresses C8's primitive: it broadcasts each step's trajectories to all workers to synchronize their local suffix caches, because per-worker trees cannot share generated patterns. This is cross-worker suffix-cache sharing by replication, not routing. Global scheduler routes on KV-cache locality, not draft-cache content.
does_not_prove: Setting is synchronous RL rollouts (same model, trusted, no tenants), not multi-tenant serving; reports no number isolating the gain from suffix sharing vs the full WAR system (1.4-1.6x combined).
bearing: C8 scoop/novelty: cross-worker suffix sharing already done by broadcast in RL; serving routing-by-affinity still open

title: BubbleSpec: sharded suffix indices across rollout DP ranks
quote: each rollout DP rank builds and maintains suffix indices only for the prompts it is responsible for generating
proves: Confirms the sharded-by-dispatch design point for C8: indices follow existing rollout dispatch; drafts are dispatched to the rank owning the prompt. Affinity is by prompt ownership, not a learned draft-cache router.
does_not_prove: RL rollout context, not serving; no comparison of random vs affinity sharding loss/recovery in a serving setting.
bearing: C8: sharding-by-dispatch exists in RL; serving affinity-routing comparison still unfilled

title: DAS: per-problem suffix shards beat a single global index
quote: A single, ever-growing global index over all past rollouts fails along both statistical and systems axes.
proves: Evidence that a single global tree is NOT always best: problem-scoped shards exceed global in acceptance and are cheaper to query; global+request is slower due to querying/maintaining one large index. Partitioning the tree can raise acceptance, not only lower it.
does_not_prove: RL rollouts with policy drift, which hurts global more than stationary serving traffic; no serving/multi-tenant numbers; acceptance deltas only in figures, not text.
bearing: C5/C8: undercuts the premise that partitioning only costs acceptance; here partitioning HELPS

title: Leaky Language Models: Stealing Architecture and Inference Optimizations via Per-Token Timing
proves: Remote per-token timing already leaks whether speculative decoding is on and the draft context length (e.g. Gemini Flash 2.5 ~128K draft window), and architecture params in top-10 >90%. Shows spec-decode timing is observable through real remote APIs.
does_not_prove: Leaks model/deployment metadata, not another tenant's content; does not touch shared draft caches.
bearing: C5 relevance: spec-decode timing is remotely observable, but this attack targets metadata not content

title: Mistletoe: Stealthy Acceleration-Collapse Attacks on Speculative Decoding
quote: a stealthy acceleration-collapse attack against speculative decoding
proves: 2026 follow-up to Speculation-Spills-Secrets lineage targets availability (collapse acceptance while preserving output), not confidentiality. Confirms the active research frontier on spec-decode attacks is acceptance-collapse, not cross-tenant content leakage.
does_not_prove: Does not attack suffix/n-gram or shared draft caches, and is an availability not a confidentiality attack.
bearing: C5 novelty: nearby 2026 spec-decode attacks are availability, leaving the content-leak-via-shared-draft-cache gap open

title: Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks on Speculative Decoding
proves: Another Oct-2026 spec-decode attack: adversarial suffixes lower acceptance to slow a victim, transferable across drafters/targets. Confirms attack interest in acceptance but again on availability, via a model-drafter not a shared cache.
does_not_prove: No confidentiality/leakage; no shared draft cache; model-based drafters, not suffix/n-gram.
bearing: C5 novelty/scoop: reinforces that the cross-tenant draft-cache leak is still unaddressed
